body.text: Even before Democrats regained control of the U.S. Congress in the 2026 midterms, leftist foreign policy analysts began to set forth a series of arguments about what a progressive foreign policy agenda might look like. One of these efforts resulted in the book “A World For All: New Visions of U.S. Foreign Policy,” edited by Matthew Duss of the Center for International Policy (full disclosure: I co-authored the chapter in the book about space policy).

Progressive views are in the ascendancy in the Democratic foreign policy caucus, with many voters and lawmakers frustrated with the Biden administration’s approach to Gaza and uncertain that the Obama-era consensus can be rebuilt. While progressives have long taken an outsider perspective on U.S. foreign policy, critiquing both the national security state and the nature of U.S. economic integration with the global economic order, they now have sufficient leverage in Congress and elsewhere to help establish new foreign policy priorities.

The book is a collection of essays from well-known authors and analysts on the progressive left. As such, while there is no single point of view, it does offer a coherent sense of how the progressive left will adapt to the realities of U.S. power and influence. The core insight with respect to Asia is that the establishment of Cold War dynamics between Beijing and Washington will be bad for everything that progressives hold dear. This includes the expansion of the national security and surveillance states domestically, the expansion of military budgets, and the creation of dangerous dynamics of escalation that could lead to unnecessary military conflict.

China is, of course, not the only focus of the book. “A World For All” includes insights on trade and the environment, where a progressive approach would attempt to lock in domestic labor, product standards, and environmental protections in order to avoid race-to-the-bottom dynamics. It also establishes climate change as a key pillar of U.S. foreign policy in Asia, for which cooperation between the United States, China, Japan, and India is absolutely critical.

Nevertheless, the argument correctly identifies the potential for competition with China to become the guiding principle of U.S. foreign policy, a principle that would lead down the same rocky road as American Cold War relations with the Soviet Union. A progressive approach envisions continuing partnerships with traditional U.S. allies such as Japan and South Korea, but understanding those partnerships as values in and of themselves rather than as tools to contain China.

And indeed this may offer the biggest caveat to the progressive vision for foreign policy. Every vision of American foreign policy involves placing China in some kind of box; hawks want to put China in a small box where it can be confined and constrained, while progressives want to give China a larger box in the hopes of avoiding unnecessarily destructive competition. Progressives hope that the United States can undertake policies that will shape Chinese behavior and establish productive guardrails on competition that will reduce China’s sense of insecurity. But if China does not wish to remain in that box and does not want to have its behavior shaped, then these steps may be for naught. As with Russia and the United States, China’s foreign policy rests on ideological impulses as well as structural factors, meaning that China gets a vote on how competition in the Pacific plays out.

Most importantly, the impulse to bring ideology back into foreign policy is a good one. Partisan politics have never stopped at the water’s edge, and the best efforts of the foreign policy community to depoliticize foreign policy have led to groupthink and catastrophe. Developing explicitly ideological foundations for the behavior of the United States on the world stage allows for a much richer and more involved conversation about how the United States conducts its foreign relations.
